q: The energy carried by a single photon is directly proportional to the light's:
x: E = hf, so photon energy rises in direct proportion to frequency. It is inversely proportional to wavelength and does not depend on amplitude.

q: One electronvolt, a unit often used for photon energies, is equal to:
x: 1 eV is the energy gained by an electron moved through 1 V: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 1 V = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

q: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 330 nm falls on a surface. How much energy does each photon deliver? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: E = hc/λ = (6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(3.3 × 10⁻⁷) = 6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Forgetting to convert nm to m gives the 10⁻²⁸ value.

q: In the particle model of light, the momentum of a photon of wavelength λ is:
x: A photon's momentum is p = E/c = hf/c = h/λ, even though its rest mass is zero.

q: Two photons have energies in the ratio 1 : 4. The ratio of their wavelengths is:
x: E = hc/λ, so wavelength is inversely proportional to energy. Energies 1 : 4 give wavelengths 4 : 1.

q: Which list puts these photons in order of increasing energy?
o: Radio waves, infrared, visible light, X-rays
X-rays, visible light, infrared, radio waves
Infrared, radio waves, X-rays, visible light
Visible light, infrared, X-rays, radio waves
x: Photon energy increases with frequency. Radio waves have the lowest frequency, then infrared, visible light and X-rays.

q: The intensity of a beam of monochromatic light is doubled while its frequency is kept the same. What happens to the photons?
o: Each photon has twice the energy, with the same number per second
Each photon has half the energy, with four times as many per second
Each photon moves at twice the speed
Each photon has the same energy, but twice as many arrive per second
x: Photon energy depends only on frequency (E = hf). A brighter beam simply carries more photons per second.

q: Electrons are only just released from a surface whose work function is 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the longest wavelength of light able to do this? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: Threshold wavelength λ₀ = hc/φ = (1.98 × 10⁻²⁵)/(6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 3 × 10⁻⁷ m = 300 nm. Longer wavelengths carry too little energy per photon.

q: A surface lit by 6 eV photons releases electrons with up to 3.5 eV of kinetic energy. How much energy is needed just to free an electron from it?
x: From hf = φ + KEmax, φ = 6 − 3.5 = 2.5 eV. Adding the two energies (9.5 eV) is the usual slip.

q: Photons of energy 4.5 eV fall on a metal with work function 2.5 eV. The stopping potential needed to halt the fastest photoelectrons is:
x: KEmax = 4.5 − 2.5 = 2 eV, and eV₀ = KEmax, so the stopping potential is 2 V.

q: The wave theory of light fails to explain the photoelectric effect because it predicts that:
o: Light of any frequency should eject electrons if it is intense enough
Electrons should be emitted only above a threshold frequency
The maximum kinetic energy should rise with frequency
x: On the wave picture, energy depends on intensity, so even low-frequency light should work if bright enough. Experiments show a threshold frequency, which the photon model explains.

q: Light above the threshold frequency is switched on and falls on a metal. Photoelectrons are observed:
o: Only after the metal has absorbed energy for several minutes
Practically instantly, with no measurable delay
Only after the metal becomes hot
After a delay that is longer for brighter light
x: Each electron absorbs a whole photon in a single event, so emission starts at once. A delay would be expected only if energy built up gradually, as in the wave picture.

q: When the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is plotted against frequency, the point where the straight line cuts the frequency axis gives the:
x: KEmax = hf − hf₀ is zero when f = f₀, so the line meets the frequency axis at the threshold frequency. Its slope, not its intercept, is h.

q: Graphs of maximum photoelectron kinetic energy against light frequency are drawn for two metals with different work functions. The two straight lines are:
o: Parallel, with different intercepts on the frequency axis
Of different slopes, passing through the same point
x: Each slope equals h, the same for every metal, so the lines are parallel. Different work functions give different threshold frequencies, hence different intercepts.

q: A laser emits 2 × 10¹⁸ photons per second, each of energy 3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Its power output is:
x: Power = number per second × energy each = 2 × 10¹⁸ × 3 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.6 W.

q: Ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 200 nm shines on a surface that needs 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J to free an electron. With what largest kinetic energy do electrons emerge? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
The scientist who explained the photoelectric effect by treating light as a stream of photons was:
x: Einstein (1905) applied Planck's quantum idea to light itself, explaining the threshold frequency and his photoelectric equation hf = φ + KEmax.

q: Light whose photons carry 3 eV shines on a surface with a 2 eV work function. Doubling the light's frequency changes the energy of the fastest ejected electrons to:
x: Originally KEmax = 3 − 2 = 1 eV. Doubling frequency gives 6 eV photons, so KEmax = 6 − 2 = 4 eV, which is 4 times the original, not simply double.
